Take-Home_Ex03

Installing and Loading R packages

pacman::p_load(httr, tidyverse, sf, tmap, 
               jsonlite, progress, gtsummary, performance, RColorBrewer, sfdep, GWmodel)

Geocoding HDB resale data

Selecting data of interest

We will filter out 3 room, 4 room and 5 room flats

HDBresale <- read_csv(
  "data/rawdata/HDBresale.csv") %>%
  filter(flat_type %in% c("3 ROOM", "4 ROOM", "5 ROOM")) %>%
  filter(month >= "2025-09" & month < "2025-10")
Rows: 218874 Columns: 11
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (8): month, town, flat_type, block, street_name, storey_range, flat_mode...
dbl (3): floor_area_sqm, lease_commence_date, resale_price

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

We will create a function that helps us convert the address into latitude and longitude using OneMapSG api.

geocode <- function(block, streetname) {
  base_url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"
  address <- paste(block, streetname, sep = " ")
  query <- list("searchVal" = address, 
                "returnGeom" = "Y",
                "getAddrDetails" = "N",
                "pageNum" = "1")
  
  res <- GET(base_url, query = query)
  restext<-content(res, as="text")
  
  output <- fromJSON(restext)  %>% 
    as.data.frame %>%
    select(results.LATITUDE, results.LONGITUDE)

  return(output)
}

Now we will use that function

HDBresale$LATITUDE <- 0
HDBresale$LONGITUDE <- 0

for (i in 1:nrow(HDBresale)){
  temp_output <- geocode(HDBresale[i, 4], HDBresale[i, 5])
  
  HDBresale$LATITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LATITUDE
  HDBresale$LONGITUDE[i] <- temp_output$results.LONGITUDE
}

We have the columns Latitude and Longitude.

Proximity Analysis

Count number of geographic entities located within a defined distance of each HDB

Let’s count the number of preschools located within 350m of each resale HDB

Convert hdb resale to sf

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale %>%
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
    crs=4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Counting number of preschools

within_350m <- st_is_within_distance(
  HDBresale_sf, preschool, dist = 350)

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(WITHIN_350M_PRISCHOOL = map_int(within_350m, length))

Computing shortest distance

nearest_dist <- function(from_geom, to_sf) {
  as.numeric(
    st_distance(
      from_geom,
      to_sf[st_nearest_feature(from_geom, to_sf), ],
      by_element = TRUE
    )
  )
}

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(
    PROX_PRESCHOOL     = nearest_dist(geometry, preschool),
    PROX_CHASCLINIC    = nearest_dist(geometry, CHASclinic),
    PROX_CHILDCARE     = nearest_dist(geometry, childCareServices),
    PROX_HAWKER        = nearest_dist(geometry, hawkerCenters),
    PROX_PARK          = nearest_dist(geometry, parks),
    PROX_SUPERMARKET   = nearest_dist(geometry, supermarkets),
    PROX_ELDERCARE     = nearest_dist(geometry, eldercare),
  )

13.7 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

13.7.1 EDA using statistical graphics

ggplot(data=HDBresale_sf, 
       aes(x=`resale_price`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

Right skewed meaning more hdb flats were transacted at lower relative prices.

Normalize the resale price using a new variable called log_resale_price by using a log transformation on the variable resale_price It is performed using mutate() of dplyr package.

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(`log_resale_price` = log(resale_price))
ggplot(data=HDBresale_sf, 
       aes(x=`log_resale_price`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, 
                 color="black", 
                 fill="light blue")

distribution is relatively less skewed after the transformation.

13.8 Hedonic Pricing Modelling in R

building hedonic pricing models for HDB units using lm() of R base

13.8.1 Simple Linear Regression Method

First, we will build a simple linear regression model by using resale_price as the dependent variable and floor_area_sqm as the independent variable.

HDBslr <- lm(formula=resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm,
             data = HDBresale_sf)

lm() returns an object of class “lm” or for multiple responses of class c(“mlm”, “lm”).

The functions summary() and anova() can be used to obtain and print a summary and analysis of variance table of the results. The generic accessor functions coefficients, effects, fitted.values and residuals extract various useful features of the value returned by lm.

summary(HDBslr)

Call:
lm(formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm, data = HDBresale_sf)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-287752 -105474  -47412   55688  857295 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    122664.9    19008.0   6.453 1.37e-10 ***
floor_area_sqm   5701.3      196.8  28.969  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 165500 on 1970 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2987,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2984 
F-statistic: 839.2 on 1 and 1970 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

The output report reveals that the SELLING_PRICE can be explained by using the formula:

      *y = 122664.9 + 5701.3x*

The R-squared of 0.2987 reveals that the simple regression model built is able to explain about 29% of the resale prices.

Since p-value is much smaller than 0.0001, we will reject the null hypothesis that mean is a good estimator of resale_price. This will allow us to infer that simple linear regression model above is a good estimator of resale_price.

The Coefficients: section of the report reveals that the p-values of both the estimates of the Intercept and floor_area_sqm are smaller than 0.001. In view of this, the null hypothesis of the B0 and B1 are equal to 0 will be rejected. As a results, we will be able to infer that the B0 and B1 are good parameter estimates.

To visualise the best fit curve on a scatterplot, we can incorporate lm() as a method function in ggplot’s geometry as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=HDBresale_sf,  
       aes(x=`floor_area_sqm`, y=`resale_price`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Figure above reveals that there are a few statistical outliers with relatively high selling prices.

13.8.2 Multiple Linear Regression Method

13.8.2.1 Visualising the relationships of the independent variables

Before building a multiple regression model, it is important to ensure that the indepdent variables used are not highly correlated to each other. If these highly correlated independent variables are used in building a regression model by mistake, the quality of the model will be compromised. This phenomenon is known as multicollinearity in statistics.

The code chunk below is used to plot a scatterplot matrix of the relationship between the independent variables in HDBresale data.frame.

But before that we need to clean up some of our varaiables

Calculate age:

library(stringr)
library(dplyr)

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract years and months  
    lease_years  = as.numeric(str_extract(remaining_lease, "\\d+(?= years?)")),
    lease_months = as.numeric(str_extract(remaining_lease, "\\d+(?= months?)")),
    lease_months = ifelse(is.na(lease_months), 0, lease_months),
    
    # Convert to years
    remaining_lease_num = lease_years + lease_months / 12,
    
    # Compute AGE
    AGE = 99 - remaining_lease_num
  )

Convert flattype to numeric

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(
    FLAT_TYPE_NUM = case_when(
      flat_type == "1 ROOM" ~ 1,
      flat_type == "2 ROOM" ~ 2,
      flat_type == "3 ROOM" ~ 3,
      flat_type == "4 ROOM" ~ 4,
      flat_type == "5 ROOM" ~ 5,
      flat_type == "EXECUTIVE" ~ 6,
      flat_type == "MULTI-GENERATION" ~ 7,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

convert storey to numeric:

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  mutate(
    storey_low  = as.numeric(str_extract(storey_range, "^\\d+")),
    storey_high = as.numeric(str_extract(storey_range, "\\d+$")),
    STOREY_MID  = (storey_low + storey_high) / 2
  )
library(corrplot)
corrplot 0.95 loaded
num_vars <- HDBresale_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(
    floor_area_sqm, AGE, FLAT_TYPE_NUM, STOREY_MID,
    starts_with("PROX"), 
    log_resale_price
  )

corr_matrix <- cor(num_vars, use = "complete.obs")

corrplot(corr_matrix,diag = FALSE, 
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td", 
         tl.cex = 0.5, 
         method = "number", 
         type = "upper")

            check= "normality")

The figure reveals that the residual of the multiple linear regression model (i.e. HDBmlr1) is resemble normal distribution

13.8.6.4 Testing for Spatial Autocorrelation

mlr.output <- as.data.frame(HDBmlr1$residuals)
HDBresale_sf <- cbind(HDBresale_sf, 
                        HDBmlr1$residuals) %>%
rename(`MLR_RES` = `HDBmlr1.residuals`)
tmap_mode("plot")
ℹ tmap mode set to "plot".
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.4) +
tm_shape(HDBresale_sf) +  
  tm_dots(
    fill = "MLR_RES",
    size = 0.7,
    col = "black",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(
      n = 10,
      values = rev(
        brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")),
      style = "quantile",
      midpoint = NA),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residuals")
  ) + 
  tm_title("LM Residuals (Quantile Classification)") +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11,14))
tmap_mode("plot")
ℹ tmap mode set to "plot".

The figure above reveal that there is sign of spatial autocorrelation.

To proof that our observation is indeed true, Global Moran’s I test will be performed

First, we will compute the distance-based weight matrix by using st_dist_band() function of sfdep.

HDBresale_sf <- HDBresale_sf %>% 
  mutate(
    nb = st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry), 
                 upper = 1500),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1) 
set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(
  HDBresale_sf$MLR_RES, 
  nb = HDBresale_sf$nb, 
  wt = HDBresale_sf$wt,
  alternative = "two.sided", 
  nsim = 499)

    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.42816, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

The Global Moran’s I test for residual spatial autocorrelation shows that it’s p-value is less than 0.00000000000000022 which is less than the alpha value of 0.05. Hence, we will reject the null hypothesis that the residuals are randomly distributed.

Since the Observed Global Moran I = 0.14389 which is greater than 0, we can infer than the residuals resemble cluster distribution.

    STOREY_MID + PROX_CHASCLINIC,
  data=HDBresale_sf,
  approach="CV", 
  kernel="gaussian", 
  adaptive=TRUE, 
  longlat=FALSE)
